items.content_html:
Summary

Enumerable#in_order_of with filter: false is documented to keep elements that aren't named in the series:

If the Enumerable has additional elements that aren't named in the series, these are not included in the result, unless the filter option is set to false.

But a stray compact (copied from the filter: true branch) silently removed nil elements:

[3, nil, 1, 2].in_order_of(:itself, [1, 2, 3], filter: false)
# => [1, 2, 3]        (before — nil dropped)
# => [1, 2, 3, nil]   (after  — nil preserved)

Why the compact is wrong here

The filter: true branch needs compact because group_by(&key).values_at(*series) produces nil for series entries with no matching element. The filter: false branch uses sort_by, which never introduces nil, so the compact only stripped genuine nil elements from the collection — contradicting the documented contract.

Changes

  • Remove the compact from the filter: false branch.
  • Add a regression test.
  • CHANGELOG entry.

All existing activesupport enumerable_test.rb tests pass.
items.title: Fix Enumerable#in_order_of dropping nil elements when filter: false

items.content_html:
Summary

The default_order: association option (added by aa76590, merged 2026-05-28 and not yet in a released version) is silently ignored on the normal association load path.

class Author < ApplicationRecord
  has_many :posts, default_order: "posts.id DESC"
end

author = Author.first

author.posts.to_sql          # => "... ORDER BY posts.id DESC"   ✅
author.posts.pluck(:id)      # => [6, 5, 4, 2, 1]                ✅
author.posts.to_a.map(&:id)  # => [1, 2, 4, 5, 6]   ❌  arbitrary DB order
author.posts.map(&:id)       # => [1, 2, 4, 5, 6]   ❌

So the generated SQL advertises an ORDER BY while the materialized collection comes back in arbitrary database order — a silent wrong-result.

Cause

CollectionAssociation#scope applies the option (scope.default_order!(options[:default_order]), collection_association.rb:305), so building a relation via pluck/count/to_sql does emit the ORDER BY.

But Association#find_target only uses self.scope on the slow path guarded by skip_statement_cache?. On the default fast path it builds SQL from the cached statement via AssociationScope#scope, which only merges default_order_values carried by reflection scope-chain item relations (association_scope.rb:155) — it never reads options[:default_order]. A plain has_many ..., default_order: ... has no scope block and no default_scope, so skip_statement_cache? returns false and the cached, ORDER BY-less SQL loads the target.

The existing feature tests pass only because they exercise the scope path (pluck / .first) or use Comment, which has a default_scope that already forces the slow path. No test loaded the target of a plain (no-default_scope) association.

Fix

Treat a declared default_order: like a scope for statement-cache purposes, so the association loads through the scope that applies the order:

def skip_statement_cache?(scope)
  reflection.has_scope? ||
    reflection.options[:default_order].present? ||
    scope.eager_loading? ||
    klass.scope_attributes? ||
    reflection.source_reflection.active_record.default_scopes.any?
end

This is the minimal correct fix and mirrors how reflection.has_scope? already opts scoped associations out of the cache. The trade-off is that default_order: associations no longer use the statement cache; an alternative would be to carry options[:default_order] into AssociationScope so the cached SQL itself includes the ORDER BY. Happy to take that shape instead if preferred.

Test

test_default_order_is_applied_when_the_target_is_loaded in has_many_associations_test.rb adds a plain has_many :posts_with_default_order, ..., default_order: "posts.id DESC" on Author (no default_scope) and asserts the loaded target (to_a / reload) matches the SQL order, not just pluck.

Verified red on main / green with the fix. Full has_many_associations_test and relations_test green on sqlite3, postgresql, mysql2, and trilogy.

Note

Sibling bug in the same feature: reverse_order discards a relation's default_order (separate PR). The two are independent (associations layer vs relation/query_methods).
items.title: Apply `has_many` `default_order:` when the association target is loaded

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

I talked at Rails World 2025 with @dhh and @rafaelfranca about whether modules of Rails core - especially Active Storage - could be opened up to support ActiveModel-based backends other than Active Record, particularly NoSQL databases like DynamoDB, MongoDB, etc. I've designed and run quite a number of large non–Active Record applications for more than 15 years, so I genuinely believe a more open stance toward the persistence layer would benefit the Rails ecosystem.

That's the reason for this PR.

Active Storage's persistence is currently hardwired to three Active Record models - ActiveStorage::Blob, ActiveStorage::Attachment, and ActiveStorage::VariantRecord. In practice these are little more than metadata records - a service key, filename, content type, byte size, checksum, and a small metadata hash - created, looked up by id or a handful of attributes, and deleted.

That's a modest persistence need; it doesn't require the heavier machinery Active Record is built for (migrations, SQL joins, eager-loaded association graphs) - which is exactly the set of features this PR scopes out as Active Record–only. Yet the hardcoded coupling ties every Active Storage feature (attachments, direct uploads, analysis, variants, previews, purging) to a SQL database, even when an application stores the rest of its data elsewhere. Apps that pair Rails with a non-relational store today can't reuse Active Storage against it without reimplementing large parts of it.

I've already had to reimplement large parts of Active Storage for the project I'm currently working on, so this PR distills those learnings.

This PR makes those persistence classes pluggable, while keeping Active Record as the single, unchanged default - so nothing changes for existing AR Rails apps.

Details / What it does

  • Class indirection. ActiveStorage.blob_class / attachment_class / variant_record_class, configurable via config.active_storage.*, replace the hardcoded constant references throughout Active Storage.
  • Boots without Active Record. When a backend configures all three classes, Active Storage loads and runs without Active Record present (Active Storage now depends on Active Model rather than Active Record).
  • Generic attachment owners. Plain ActiveModel objects can declare has_one_attached / has_many_attached, going through a non-AR builder that mirrors the Active Record dependent-purge/commit semantics without requiring a database transaction.
  • Documented contracts. A new guide - Custom Active Storage Backends - specifies exactly what a custom Blob / Attachment / VariantRecord and a non-AR owner must implement.
  • A reference backend (in-memory) exercises the whole contract in the test suite.

Opting in

A backend should normally be shipped as a gem: it points Active Storage at its classes from a Railtie, and applications just add the gem and declare attachments. The owner's .find, #id, #persisted?, and :save/:destroy/:commit callbacks come from its own persistence layer - they aren't hand-written.

In an application (using a backend gem):

# Gemfile
gem "activestorage-aws-record"   # example backend; its Railtie sets blob/attachment/variant_record_class

# app/models/message.rb
class Message
  include Aws::Record                       # the datastore: supplies #id, #persisted?, .find
  include ActiveStorage::AwsRecord::Owner   # contract glue (callbacks) from the backend gem
  string_attr :id, hash_key: true

  has_one_attached  :avatar
  has_many_attached :images
end

A record that already manages its own persistence (versioning, events, search) just include ActiveStorage::Attached::Model and declares attachments - the callbacks it already defines satisfy the contract.

Building a backend gem - implement the Blob / Attachment / VariantRecord contract and point Active Storage at it, before active_storage.class_indirection:

initializer "my_backend.active_storage", before: "active_storage.class_indirection" do |app|
  app.config.active_storage.blob_class           = "MyBackend::Blob"
  app.config.active_storage.attachment_class     = "MyBackend::Attachment"
  app.config.active_storage.variant_record_class = "MyBackend::VariantRecord"
end

The Custom Active Storage Backends guide has all the details; the DynamoDB adapter linked below is a complete reference.

Backward compatibility (the important part)

  • Zero behavior change for existing apps. With Active Record loaded and the default classes in use (the default), every path is identical. The new "ignore the default AR model files" initializer is a literal no-op in that configuration - it only acts when no AR is present or a custom backend is configured.
  • Entirely opt-in. No new default behavior; you get the new path only by configuring all three classes.
  • Dependency change to flag: the activestorage gemspec now declares activemodel instead of activerecord. Apps on the default AR backend still get Active Record through the Rails meta-gem / their own Gemfile (and activerecord pulls in activemodel). This is the change that lets Active Storage load without Active Record - explicitly calling it out for review.
  • Hybrid is explicitly unsupported. Mixing Active Record owners with custom storage classes raises ActiveStorage::HybridConfigurationError; partial configuration raises ActiveStorage::ConfigurationError. Failures are loud and early (boot/declaration time), never silent.

Intentionally out of scope (documented limitations)

  • with_attached_* raises EagerLoadingNotSupported; strict_loading: true raises ArgumentError.
  • Active Storage fixtures remain Active Record–specific.
  • MirrorService targets the default Active Record blob service.
  • SQL-join-based features apply only to the Active Record backend.

Commit structure

Six focused, easily reviewable commits:

  1. Extract the Active Storage attachment builder
  2. Add Active Storage class indirection
  3. Make Active Storage boot without Active Record
  4. Ignore the default Active Record model files when running without Active Record
  5. Add generic Active Storage attachment owners
  6. Test and document generic Active Storage attachment owners

Testing

  • activestorage: 662 runs, 2114 assertions, 0 failures (BUNDLE_WITHOUT=db bin/test).
  • railties: a no–Active Record boot test (runs in a clean subprocess so the AR-loaded harness can't leak in) and an Active-Record-present-with-custom-backend eager-load test.
  • The in-memory reference backend covers attach / download / detach / purge / direct upload / analyze / variant tracking through the concrete custom classes.

Example adapter

I built a working DynamoDB adapter as a proof of the contract: https://github.com/thomaswitt/activestorage-aws-record … FYI, the adapter is in production testing right now and working without issues so far.

Checklist

Before submitting the PR make sure the following are checked:

  • This Pull Request is related to one change. Unrelated changes should be opened in separate PRs.
  • Commit message has a detailed description of what changed and why. If this PR fixes a related issue include it in the commit message. Ex: [Fix #issue-number]
  • Tests are added or updated if you fix a bug or add a feature.
  • CHANGELOG files are updated for the changed libraries if there is a behavior change or additional feature. Minor bug fixes and documentation changes should not be included.
items.title: Allow Active Storage to use non–Active Record persistence backends

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

While migrating my app from SQLite to Postgres some time ago, I've noticed some inconsistencies in how the precision is set in timestamp columns depending on how they're declared in the migration DSL. I made an example repo here that demonstrates the problem: https://github.com/mackuba/rails-timestamp-precision-demo.

It creates a table with 3 sets of 4 timestamp fields each: datetime, timestamp, and timestamptz, with precision set to 0, 6, nil and not specified. These columns all end up as either timestamp or timestamptz in the database, since datetime maps to one of those depending on the datetime_type setting, but where they differ is in the precision flags. I would have expected the 4 precision options to end up with the same result in each of the 3 sets, but they don't:

  • the timestamptz set of columns have no precision at all, none of the 4 fields
  • the timestamp and timestamptz with no precision set default to a precision nil, instead of 6 as datetime does

Note, this is all Postgres specific, since in MySQL datetime and timestamp are two very different column types.

Detail

I've made a number of fixes in:

  • ActiveRecord::ConnectionAdapters::PostgreSQL::SchemaStatements#type_to_sql
  • ActiveRecord::ConnectionAdapters::PostgreSQL::ColumnMethods::TableDefinition#new_column_definition
  • ActiveRecord::ConnectionAdapters::PostgreSQL::SchemaDumper#schema_precision

which make the precision behave the same across Postgres columns declared as datetime, timestamp and timestamptz, both with datetime_type set to :timestamptz and with the default setting, in how the schema.rb is written and in what actually ends up in the database structure. Plus I've added some tests that I think should cover all of this.

Additional information

I made all the changes in the PostgreSQL subclasses of the components, since these are all Postgres-specific things. Alternatively, some changes could be made in the abstract base class instead, e.g. the first commit could just be replaced with adding :timestamptz here to the base SchemaStatements:

elsif [:datetime, :timestamp, :time, :interval].include?(type) && precision ||= native[:precision]

since the :interval, which I think is also Postgres-specific, is already there. But it felt more appropriate to put it in the Postgres subclasses.

We could also move the :interval from there to the Postgres subclass now for consistency.

One thing to note is that this will create diffs in some people's schema.rb on update and after regenerating the schema, because of the changed defaults:

  • if someone had a t.timestamptz field (or a t.timestamp field in datetime_type = :timestamptz mode), it would have no precision and be printed to schema.rb with no precision option, but now it will be dumped as ..., precision: nil, since the default will now be 6
  • in datetime_type = :timestamptz mode, if someone had a t.timestamp field with precision: 6, it will be dumped to schema.rb with the option omitted since that's now the default as in datetime
items.title: Fix handling of `precision` in timestamp columns in Postgres migrations

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

This Pull Request has been created because the CreateOrFindByWithinTransactions test was incorrectly wrapping find_or_create_by calls inside an outer Subscriber.transaction block. This caused create_or_find_by's internal transaction to be demoted to a savepoint, which broke MySQL's error recovery path: when a uniqueness conflict triggered a savepoint rollback, MySQL had already invalidated the savepoint due to the transaction-level lock error (errno 1020), resulting in a SAVEPOINT active_record_1 does not exist failure.

Detail

This Pull Request removes the outer Subscriber.transaction wrapper from the duel helper in the test. find_or_create_by now runs its own top-level transaction as intended, so MySQL can properly roll it back on conflict and the rescue/retry logic in create_or_find_by works correctly.

Additional information

The failure manifested as two chained errors on MySQL/Trilogy:

  • 1020: Record has changed since last read (optimistic locking conflict on INSERT)
  • 1305: SAVEPOINT active_record_1 does not exist (cascading from the above)

The test passes on SQLite (already skipped) and was only reliably reproducible under
concurrent load with REPEATABLE READ isolation.

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

This PR extracts the affected_rows checking from Locking::Optimistic into a generally useful reader previously_affected_rows.

Being able to access previously_affected_rows at the instance level unlocks the ability to write granular optimistic locking behavior using the more-recently added scoping(all_queries) (#41397) behavior e.g.

post = Post.last

old_body = post.body
Post.where(body: old_body).scoping(all_queries: true) do
  record.update(body: “new_body”)
end

oops_the_body_already_changed! if previously_affected_rows.zero?

This is different from Locking::Optimistic which only allows for a single change counter for the entire record.

While it’s possible to do something similar using update_all I really wanted to be able to use this behavior at the AR instance level.

Detail

This change extracts the row-counting behavior that exists in Locking::Optimistic into AR Persistence and refactors/simplifies Locking::Optimistic to use the new behavior.

Additional information

  • I exposed previously_affected_rows to the public interface of an AR record. I could also imagine it only being populatd within the context of an around_save. That would add a little more work to express usable behavior, but no objection if we wanted to limit it
  • I think previously_affected_rows is a consistent name with analogous functionality (previously new_record?), but it does slightly leak the abstraction of “affected_rows” . Naming is hard.

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

abstract_adapter.rb with default settings has a race condition. Rails 7.1 introduced a regression in #46519 by assuming that connections are never shared across threads. In practice, that assumption doesn't always hold, especially in applications that use a connection pool together with RDS Proxy. PostgreSQLAdapter requires a lock since type_map is initialized lazily, a change made in #44570.

Cross-referencing #51780 (comment).

Detail

Add a connection_lock database config for applications that share a connection across threads or fibers. When enabled, ActiveRecord locks the adapter during reconnect and PostgreSQL result processing so a shared connection cannot be used while it is being reconnected.

I noticed that some type_map readers were not guarded, I added @lock.synchronize in a few additional places. I am leaving this to your best judgement since that work ballooned beyond connection_pool, abstract_adapter, and postgresql_adapter classes, and I am less familiar with database_statements class.

Additional information

Repro of the original issue:

$ cat Gemfile
ruby "3.3.4"
gem "activerecord", "=8.1.3"

$ cat database.yml
development:
  adapter: postgresql
  url: postgres://localhost:5432/giza_development
  database: giza_development
  username: postgres
  gssencmode: disable
  pool: 5

$ cat repro.rb
require "active_record"
require "yaml"
config = YAML.load(File.read("database.yml"))["development"]
ActiveRecord::Base.establish_connection(config)
Thread.abort_on_exception = true
ActiveRecord::Base.connection_pool.with_connection do |connection|
  Thread.new(connection) do |pg|
    pg.reconnect!
  end
  p connection.select_values("SELECT 1")
end

$ irb -r ./repro.rb
/opt/homebrew/lib/ruby/gems/3.3.0/gems/activerecord-8.1.3/lib/active_record/connection_adapters/postgresql_adapter.rb:876:in `get_oid_type': undefined method `key?' for nil (NoMethodError)

          if !type_map.key?(oid)
                      ^^^^^

After the following patch is applied, the error is no longer reproducible:

module ActiveRecord::ConnectionAdapters::PostgreSQLAdapterPatch
  def initialize(
    config_or_deprecated_connection,
    deprecated_logger = nil,
    deprecated_connection_options = nil,
    deprecated_config = nil
  )
    super
    @lock = ActiveSupport::Concurrency::ThreadMonitor.new
  end
end

class ActiveRecord::ConnectionAdapters::PostgreSQLAdapter
  prepend ActiveRecord::ConnectionAdapters::PostgreSQLAdapterPatch
end

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

config.active_storage.service_urls_expire_in and config.active_storage.urls_expire_in are stored as module-level state (mattr_accessor on ActiveStorage) and read directly wherever URLs are generated (Blob#url, Variant#url, the redirect controllers' Cache-Control header, and the rails_storage_* route helpers for signed-id expiry).

In a multi-tenant application that needs a different URL expiry per tenant, there is no hook to vary these values at request time without monkey-patching Blob#signed_id and the redirect controller.

Detail

This makes both readers resolve a callable on read: if the configured value responds to call, it is invoked and the result is used. Because every consumption site already reads ActiveStorage.service_urls_expire_in / ActiveStorage.urls_expire_in, the resolution propagates without touching Blob, Variant, the routes, or the controllers.

config.active_storage.service_urls_expire_in = -> { Current.tenant&.url_expiry || 5.minutes }

Fully backward compatible: ActiveSupport::Duration, Integer and nil do not respond to call, so they pass through unchanged.

Additional information

Includes a unit test for both readers, integration tests proving the callable is resolved end-to-end (signed-id expiry and the Cache-Control header), a CHANGELOG entry, and guide docs.
items.title: Allow Active Storage URL expiry to be configured with a callable

Motivation / Background

Follow-up to #57479. Seeking feedback on whether this conflict detection is worth adding.

In a multi-database app, sharing a single migration base class across different adapter types (e.g. PostgreSQL primary + MySQL secondary) silently accumulates conflicting compatibility modules. This can cause one adapter's defaults to leak into another's migration runs.

Detail

Add ActiveRecord::Migration::Compatibility::ConflictError, raised when a migration base class is associated with compatibility behavior from more than one adapter type. The error message recommends using a distinct migration base class per adapter type. Single-adapter applications are unaffected.

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

Adapter-specific migration compatibility logic was scattered across a single monolithic Compatibility class with adapter_name string comparisons. This made it hard to maintain and impossible for third-party adapters to extend without monkey-patching (e.g. cockroachdb adapter, oracle-enhanced #2596, oracle-enhanced #2710).

Detail

Each built-in adapter now defines its own MigrationCompatibility module and returns it from the new migration_compatibility_module_for hook. Third-party adapters can override this hook to ship per-version legacy behavior without patching Rails internals.

The hook is registered on Mysql2Adapter and TrilogyAdapter (not AbstractMysqlAdapter) so third-party adapters subclassing the abstract class are not implicitly opted in.

Additional information

Verified that the CockroachDB adapter's monkey patch is no longer needed — migration_compatibility_module_for is inherited from PostgreSQLAdapter, and :datetime → :timestamp conversion works correctly for Migration[6.1] on CockroachDB without any adapter-side patching.

Checklist

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

This Pull Request has been created because some intermediate query proxies (e.g. PgDog) struggle with very large WHERE IN (...) clauses produced when preloading associations on large record sets. There is currently no way to limit the number of IDs per preloader query without monkey-patching Rails.

Also, some preload queries just timeout because the large number of rows being preloaded.

Detail

This Pull Request changes the LoaderQuery#load_records_for_keys method in ActiveRecord::Associations::Preloader to respect a new ActiveRecord.preload_batch_size setting. When the value is nil (the default), the behavior is identical to before, all keys are loaded in a single query. When set to an integer, the keys are split in batches and one query is issued per batch, with results merged at the end.

  # config/application.rb
  config.active_record.preload_batch_size = 1000

Additional information

In an ideal scenario, the right fix is to avoid loading thousands of records and preloading associations all at once, but in a large, actively maintained application that is not always immediately feasible. This option provides a safe escape hatch while those query patterns are improved.

Checklist

Before submitting the PR make sure the following are checked:

  • This Pull Request is related to one change. Unrelated changes should be opened in separate PRs.
  • Commit message has a detailed description of what changed and why. If this PR fixes a related issue include it in the commit message. Ex: [Fix #issue-number]
  • Tests are added or updated if you fix a bug or add a feature.
  • CHANGELOG files are updated for the changed libraries if there is a behavior change or additional feature. Minor bug fixes and documentation changes should not be included.
